newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-W.Australia energy output seen on growth path.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-W.Australia energy output seen on growth path.

text.p: The Western Australian government's Office of Energy predicted primary energy production in the state will grow at an average annual rate of 3.7 percent for the next 15 years to about 2,100 petajoules (PJ) by 2009/10.

In its latest Energy Western Australia publication, the Office of Energy forecast primary energy demand will also increase over the same period but at the marginally faster pace of 3.8 percent a year.
This meant demand could reach about 1,100 PJ by 2009/10, compared with less than 300 PJ in 1973/74, the benchmark year in the Energy Western Australia publication.
Western Australia's fossil-fuel resources totalled 201,711 PJ at 30 June, 1995, the publication's most recent data show.
These resources included 12 identified coal fields, one of which, at Collie in the state's south-west, is currently being mined, and five sedimentary basins known to contain petroleum resources.
Three of the basins, the northern Perth Basin, Carnarvon Basin and northern Canning Basin are in production.
Primary energy production reached 1,240 PJ in 1994/95, an eight-fold increase since 1973/74, the figures show.

Thanks to the development of the North West Shelf, natural gas production had the highest growth over this period - an average annual increase of 16 percent, compared with the overall average of 11.2 percent.
Primary energy demand has more than doubled since 1973/74 at an average yearly rate of four percent, the data show.
Use of natural gas was up sharply in the last 21 years, from 32 PJ in 1973/74 to 287 PJ in 1994/95, it said.
Demand for natural gas should more than double by 2009/10, driven by gas demand for resources processing and power generation, it added. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
